sections.title: The Epstein Defense and NPA Negotiation
sections.content:
Kirkland & Ellis entered the Epstein case in 2006 when partner Jay P. Lefkowitz, a former George W. Bush White House adviser, took the lead in defending Jeffrey Epstein against federal prosecution in the Southern District of Florida. The defense team operated primarily from Kirkland's New York office at 159 East 53rd Street, with additional support from the DC office. A November 8, 2007 letter from Lefkowitz to prosecutors (EFTA00013698) reveals the firm's negotiation posture: "I want to make clear at the outset that Mr. Epstein is complying fully with the Non Prosecution Agreement and that he has every intention of continuing to honor its terms in good faith." The letter also asserted that Epstein's agents had not been precluded from contacting potential witnesses, a claim prosecutors disputed.

The most revealing document in the defense record is Kirkland's 17-page submission to the Office of the Deputy Attorney General (EFTA00013811), in which the firm argued that Epstein was "a successful businessman and noted philanthropist with no prior criminal record" whose conduct "falls within heartland of historic state police powers." The submission sought to end federal involvement entirely, characterizing the victims as having lied about their ages and arguing that no interstate facility was used for inducement. A separate 10-page rebuttal of an FAUSA letter (EFTA00013801) documented that prosecutors had threatened a 53-page indictment covering 40 minors with a 188-month guideline range, and alleged improprieties in the government's selection of an attorney representative for victims.

The critical structural feature of the NPA negotiation was that both sides shared an institutional home. Alexander Acosta, the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida, had been a Kirkland associate in the DC office from 1995 to 1997—the same office where Lefkowitz was a partner. A 2018 Power Line article forwarded within the Epstein network noted that "Acosta reportedly worked out the terms of his surrender with Lefkowitz, a former colleague, at a meeting in a location far away from the prosecutor's office." Ken Starr, the former Independent Counsel and Solicitor General, was also recruited for the defense from Kirkland's offices, directly lobbying Deputy Attorney General Mark Filip in a June 19, 2008 letter (EFTA00013989). Filip would later be invoked by Epstein himself as the highest DOJ official to have approved the NPA (EFTA02612560).

Billing records (EFTA02413703) show total Kirkland fees of $3,011,064: $2,319,336 for the JEE defense through December 31, 2008; $100,000 for the FTC/DB Zwirn matter through September 2009; and $591,728 in additional billings covering the DOJ investigation ($178,165), Jane Doe 101 litigation ($173,965), and a Molyneux/Juan Pablo dispute ($10,247). Scott D. Price served as second billing attorney alongside Lefkowitz, with rates between $1,045 and $1,095 per hour. The relationship extended well beyond the formal defense: Epstein visited Kirkland's offices for a three-hour meeting on March 2, 2010, sandwiched between appointments with Peter Mandelson and Jes Staley (EFTA02428729). In April 2012, Epstein was still actively referring clients to the firm, writing: "tell frank the law firm is called kirkland, and ellis, jay lefokowitz is head of litigation." By February 2019, five months before his death, Epstein emailed Kathy Ruemmler: "why isnt kirkland and ellis defending this npa in front of marra, it is their agreement that i followed? pled, registered and paid money. do they have an obligation to defend it?" (EFTA02633736).

sections.title: The DOJ Revolving Door
sections.content:
Kirkland & Ellis maintains the most extensive personnel pipeline to the Department of Justice of any American law firm. The pattern operates across both parties but achieves its greatest density in Republican administrations, particularly during the Trump presidency. Investigation findings document a four-phase evolution: from case-by-case influence, to rule-writing, to institutional capture, to formalized alignment with executive power.

The first Trump administration represented the apex of this pipeline. Attorney General William Barr had served as Kirkland Of Counsel from 2009 and as a consultant in 2011 (advising on the BP matter), before returning as Of Counsel from 2017 to 2018. Deputy Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen was a longtime Kirkland partner who had defended Raytheon, General Motors, and the Chamber of Commerce at the firm. Brian Benczkowski, who ran the Criminal Division overseeing all corporate prosecutions, had been a Kirkland partner who represented Alfa Bank (Russia's largest private bank) in its investigation of alleged secret communications with the Trump Organization. Benczkowski received an ethics waiver to participate in the Goldman Sachs 1MDB case despite Kirkland having represented Goldman. Jeffrey Clark, who later attempted to use the DOJ to overturn the 2020 election, was a Kirkland partner from 1996 to 2018. White House Counsel Pat Cipollone and deputies Patrick Philbin and John Eisenberg were all former Kirkland partners. At minimum twelve former Kirkland lawyers held senior DOJ or White House positions simultaneously.

The bipartisan dimension of the revolving door, while less dense, is significant. Neil Eggleston served as Obama's White House Counsel (2014–2017) between stints as a Kirkland partner. Ali Zaidi became Biden's National Climate Advisor (2022–2025) after serving as a Kirkland partner representing fossil fuel clients including Mission Coal, Murray Energy, and Blackstone. Richard Cordray, the first Director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, was Kirkland Of Counsel. Susan Davies, a Kirkland partner who represented Facebook in antitrust, was considered for Biden's AAG for Antitrust.

Beyond the DOJ, Kirkland alumni have occupied positions across the federal government. John Bolton served as National Security Advisor (2018–2019) after a decade as Kirkland Of Counsel. Alex Azar served as HHS Secretary (2018–2021) after working as a Kirkland associate. Brett Kavanaugh was a Kirkland partner (1997–1998, 1999–2001) before his appointment to the D.C. Circuit and subsequent elevation to the Supreme Court. Christopher Landau was a Kirkland partner for 25 years before serving as Ambassador to Mexico. Steven Bradbury, a Kirkland litigation partner from 1993 to 2004, led the Office of Legal Counsel during the torture memos era and was confirmed as Deputy Secretary of Transportation in March 2025. In the second Trump term, Eisenberg was confirmed as AAG for National Security in June 2025, extending Kirkland's presence into the current administration alongside the firm's $125 million pro bono arrangement.

sections.title: Corporate Criminal Defense and the Filip Memo
sections.content:
Mark Filip is the central figure in understanding Kirkland's corporate criminal defense practice. As Deputy Attorney General from 2008 to 2009, Filip authored the "Filip Memorandum" (August 28, 2008), which revised DOJ guidelines for corporate prosecutions to protect attorney-client privilege during investigations. He then joined Kirkland in May 2009 and spent the next fifteen years deploying the very framework he wrote to defend corporations facing the same DOJ he had led. His former chief of staff, Brian Benczkowski, co-counseled these cases at Kirkland before serving as AAG for the Criminal Division (2018–2020), then returning to the firm.

The scale of Filip's defense work at Kirkland is unprecedented. BP Deepwater Horizon (2012): Kirkland led the criminal defense that resulted in a $4.525 billion settlement—then the largest criminal resolution in U.S. history. BP pleaded guilty to 14 felony counts including 11 counts of manslaughter. Critically, all four individual executives charged either had charges dropped, were acquitted, or pleaded to misdemeanors with probation; none received prison time. The corporate settlement effectively displaced individual accountability. Volkswagen Dieselgate (2015–2017): Kirkland was hired in September 2015 and guided VW through a guilty plea with a $2.8 billion criminal penalty and three-year probation with an independent compliance monitor. Boeing 737 MAX (2021): Filip personally signed the DPA on behalf of Boeing. The $2.5 billion resolution—covering a conspiracy to defraud that led to 346 deaths in two crashes—was called "one of the worst deferred prosecution agreements I have seen" by Columbia Law Professor John Coffee. No compliance monitor was imposed, a notable departure even from Kirkland's own VW precedent.

The Boeing case crystallized public concern about the revolving door when Erin Nealy Cox, the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Texas who brought the case, resigned effective January 9, 2021—the same day the DPA was filed in her district—and joined Kirkland as partner in Dallas five months later. Crash victims' families initially alleged impropriety but withdrew the claims in January 2022. Boeing later breached the DPA (2024), and the DOJ ultimately dropped the prosecution entirely under the second Trump administration in May 2025, granting Boeing a non-prosecution agreement. The American Prospect titled its analysis of the case "Blowing the Door Off Boeing's Epstein Deal," explicitly connecting the structural parallels between the two Kirkland-negotiated agreements.

Kirkland also represents Apollo Global Management in numerous private equity transactions, including fund-level portfolio acquisitions (T.D. Williamson, June 2025) and represented Caesars Entertainment Operating Company in its Chapter 11 bankruptcy—an Apollo-controlled entity. The firm represented Goldman Sachs in the 1MDB investigation while Kirkland alumni Barr and Benczkowski ran the DOJ. It serves as outside counsel to Cerberus Capital Management on multiple acquisitions. Combined with its $3 million Epstein defense, Kirkland sits at the intersection of the investigation's financial threads—Apollo (Thread 5), L Brands (Thread 2)—and its institutional ones.

sections.title: Network Position and Institutional Assessment
sections.content:
Graph analysis of the investigation database places Kirkland & Ellis third in degree centrality with 47 connections, behind only Jeffrey Epstein (278) and William Barr (66). The firm ranks fifth in betweenness centrality (0.077), tied with Leon Black, and achieves a brokerage score of 0.967—meaning 96.7% of Kirkland's neighbor connections do not otherwise exist. This makes the firm one of the most important structural bridges in the network: it connects clusters that would otherwise be isolated. The shortest path from Boeing to Epstein, for instance, runs through Kirkland.

A critical correction established during Wave 3 of the investigation concerns the nature of Kirkland's financial sector relationships. Initial analysis identified thousands of SEC EDGAR co-appearances with Deutsche Bank (7,048 filings), JPMorgan (6,593), and Blackstone (2,346) and inferred client relationships. Verification through annual reports and registration statements established that these are structural artifacts: Kirkland represents issuers and PE sponsors while these banks serve as underwriters, indenture trustees, or financial advisors in the same transactions. Deutsche Bank's 20-F and JPMorgan's 10-K contain zero Kirkland references. Blackstone's primary outside counsel is Simpson Thacher & Bartlett. Kirkland does, however, have a confirmed relationship with Deutsche Bank in specific matters: CFTC precious metals spoofing settlement ($30 million), shareholder litigation following the forex investigation, and the MidOcean Partners $1.6 billion spin-off.

The investigation's final institutional assessment identifies Kirkland's power as structural and institutional rather than financial. The Kirkland & Ellis Foundation (EIN 36-3160355) distributed $78.6 million in grants between 2006 and 2024, with zero grants flowing to any Epstein-connected entity—standard BigLaw philanthropy. The firm's lobbying portfolio (20 LDA registrations since 1999, registrant ID 21745) is notably modest for a firm of its size, with income from CBOT ($400,000 in 1999), Verizon ($40,000), and General Motors ($40,000). This modesty is itself revealing: Kirkland's real influence operates not through registered lobbying but through the revolving door to the DOJ. The firm's only known FARA registration (No. 4558, 1991–1995) was for Goodman Holdings and Anglo Irish Beef Processors, entirely unrelated to the investigation's core networks.

Michael Oren, the former Israeli Ambassador to the United States, is listed as a Kirkland consultant in LittleSis, providing a connection to the Israeli intelligence nexus (Thread 4). Kirkland's Federalist Society ties are extensive: alumni including Kavanaugh, Starr, Robert Bork, Bolton, Eisenberg, Viet Dinh (author of the USA PATRIOT Act), and Bradbury are members or speakers. Paul Clement, the former Solicitor General, left Kirkland in 2022 after the firm announced it would no longer handle Second Amendment litigation. The 2025 agreement to provide $125 million in pro bono services for Trump-approved causes, negotiated by Chairman Jon Ballis, prompted Congressional Democrats to allege potential violations of federal bribery, extortion, honest services fraud, and racketeering statutes.

sections.title: Ken Starr and the Ongoing Epstein Relationship
sections.content:
Ken Starr, the former Independent Counsel whose investigation of Bill Clinton led to impeachment proceedings, maintained a close and multifaceted relationship with Epstein that extended at least eleven years beyond the NPA, until September 2018. The relationship began during the defense itself, when Starr lobbied Deputy Attorney General Filip to drop federal involvement in the case (EFTA00013989). But the ongoing connection far exceeded attorney-client obligations.

Documented contacts include: a conference call with Henry Rosovsky of Harvard and Starr in March 2010; a lunch with Rosovsky and Starr in Cambridge on March 19, 2010; book exchanges and lunch at Epstein's Palm Beach house in November 2017; book delivery and meetings through July–September 2018. More significantly, the relationship involved active intelligence sharing. On November 27, 2016, when Starr forwarded information about JASTA (the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act) to Epstein, Epstein responded: "got it, thanks. leave it in my hands. always a treat" (EFTA02668810). On June 13, 2018, Starr coordinated quote attribution with journalist Michael Wolff through Epstein, telling him: "I gave Michael the all clear. We're going to continue to chat" (EFTA02629642). This indicates Starr used Epstein as an intermediary for managing his public statements on presidential prosecution through Wolff, who was writing about the Trump presidency.

Jay Lefkowitz's family also maintained social ties with Epstein after the conviction. Elena Lefkowitz, Jay's wife, invited Epstein to attend the HaZamir 18th Anniversary Concert at Jazz at Lincoln Center in February–March 2011, writing: "Jay and I would like to introduce you to the work of the Zamir Choral Foundation" (EFTA02536913). Their daughter was performing. This personal social engagement occurred well after Epstein's 2008 conviction and registration as a sex offender, demonstrating that the Kirkland relationship extended into the social sphere of the firm's senior partners. Epstein also referred business to the firm beyond his own matters: the Steven Sinofsky Microsoft severance negotiation (November 2012), in which Epstein actively coached legal strategy, telling Sinofsky "Push on 20 do not fold" as Price and Lefkowitz negotiated (EFTA02723303). Billing records for the Sinofsky matter show 21 hours at $1,045–$1,095/hour (EFTA02679084).

sections.title: The $125 Million Pro Bono Arrangement (2025)
sections.content:
In April 2025, Kirkland & Ellis agreed to provide $125 million in pro bono legal services for causes approved by the Trump administration. The arrangement was part of a broader $600 million deal across five major law firms (Kirkland, A&O Shearman, Simpson Thacher, Latham & Watkins, and Cadwalader), later expanding to approximately $1 billion across nine firms. Chairman Jon Ballis led the negotiations on Kirkland's behalf. The terms required pro bono work directed toward veterans, military, law enforcement, and antisemitism causes; a disavowal of "illegal DEI" practices; a merit-based hiring pledge; and a commitment to accept clients regardless of political views.

In exchange, the EEOC withdrew letters questioning the firms' diversity, equity, and inclusion hiring practices, and the firms avoided being targeted by a threatened executive order against law firms. Congressional Democrats, including Senators Blumenthal and Schiff and Representative Raskin, sent a letter to Chairman Ballis questioning whether these arrangements violate federal bribery (18 USC 201), extortion (18 USC 1951), honest services fraud (18 USC 1346), or racketeering statutes (18 USC 1962). Kirkland experienced a talent exodus in response, with associates resigning publicly and the firm withholding its 2025 partner list.

The arrangement marks the fourth phase in Kirkland's evolving relationship with executive power. Where the firm previously operated through individual alumni cycling between Kirkland and government positions, the $125 million deal represents formalized institutional alignment: a direct financial commitment from the firm itself to the administration's policy agenda, concurrent with alumni holding senior DOJ positions. This creates a structural conflict where the same institution both serves the executive branch and has former partners exercising prosecutorial authority over cases that may involve Kirkland's corporate clients.
